group_assessment.weighting: The Chang laboratory (National Cheng Kung University, from the author contributions), writing a review and opinion piece on its own Hyal-2/WWOX/Smad4 and Zfra work. Primary for those cultured-cell models, not for Wwox loss of function or neurological disease. Statements about its own models weigh as that laboratory's interpretation; statements about other groups' knockout or human data weigh as restatements.

entries.proposition: The review states that null mutations in humans and animals cause metabolic disorders among other features; the four references are two reviews, one case report and one consanguineous-family genetic study (by title and venue), none cited with a metabolic measurement here.
entries.snippet: Notably, null mutations of WWOX/Wwox gene in humans and animals lead to severe neural diseases (e.g., microcephaly, seizure, ataxia, etc.), growth retardation, metabolic disorders, developmental delay, and early death

entries.proposition: The review itself notes that WWOX-deficient newborns do not develop cancer and asks whether WWOX is a real tumour suppressor.
entries.snippet: Nevertheless, no spontaneous cancer formation has been seen in the newborns, arguing whether WWOX is a real tumor suppressor.

entries.proposition: The statement that overexpressed WWOX sequesters transcription factors in the cytoplasm is qualified by the review as not working in vivo, citing a rat nerve-injury paper for endogenous WWOX co-translocating with CREB.
entries.snippet: Nonetheless, this does not work effectively in vivo. For example, endogenous WWOX rapidly binds and co-translocates with CREB to the nuclei of injured neurons during sciatic nerve transection in rats (Li et al., 2009).
